source.title: The Geometric Wall: Manifold Structure Predicts Layerwise Sparse Autoencoder Scaling Laws
source.authors: Eslam Zaher; M. Trzaskowski; Quan Nguyen; Fred Roosta

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It measures SAE reconstruction-loss scaling with dictionary width and fits width-scaling exponents and asymptotic floors, using a different method from the original error-vector analyses. It does not compare errors token by token across SAE sizes.
record.gate_note: The paper cites earlier findings about nonlinear residuals and model-loss effects beyond equal-sized random perturbations, but does not test those findings itself. Its own relevant results concern aggregate SAE reconstruction loss, width-scaling exponents, and fitted floors.
record.test_reason: With-floor scaling fits on Gemma Scope SAEs (up to 1M width) give a positive asymptotic reconstruction floor at six layers. This tests V2's claim that the error does not vanish with scale. Its other results are geometry-to-exponent regressions, a different construct from V2's per-token predictability.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that manifold geometry, chiefly multi-scale curvature, predicts per-layer SAE width exponents, and that the coefficients transfer between Gemma 2 2B and 9B. At the six showcase layers, the fitted floor rises with curvature and intrinsic dimension, which they read as a geometry-set wall rather than a resource ceiling. They note that absolute exponents depend on the released SAEs' training schedule.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits layerwise width–sparsity scaling laws and regresses their parameters on geometric summaries; it does not use the original study’s error-vector predictability or token-level error-context comparisons.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported exponents depend on the released width-dependent SAE training schedule. Floor calibration is restricted to six showcase layers with richer width grids. The geometry-to-exponent fit varies in cross-validated performance by model and sparsity target; at 9B the curvature model's LOO R² decreases from 0.92 to 0.85 across the tested k range.

fits_no_version.finding: A layer's multi-scale curvature predicts its SAE width-scaling exponent α(k=50). LOO R² is 0.869 at 9B and 0.976 at 2B. The regression coefficients transfer between 2B and 9B (transfer R² 0.92–0.985).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layerwise SAE width-scaling exponents are predictable from activation-manifold geometry (curvature, intrinsic dimension) and transfer across model sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: At the showcase layers, the height of the fitted floor ranks with intrinsic dimension and curvature.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The size of the irreducible SAE error tracks manifold curvature and intrinsic dimension.

record.problems: Only two backbone widths are available at most layers, so floors cannot be identified there; floor results cover six showcase layers. SAEs use a width-dependent token budget, and the authors state that the reported exponents are conditional on that schedule. Geometry measures are k-NN proxies rather than direct pullback-metric computations. The study does not measure token-by-token error correspondence across SAE sizes.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Other reported regressions target scaling coefficients or checkpoint loss rather than adding a distinct direct measure of the claim’s error-scaling components.

untested.parts: Linear predictability of the SAE error vector from the input activation.
Per-token error-norm predictability across SAE sizes. Whether larger SAEs fail on the same contexts. Whether a floor exists at layers other than the six showcase layers.
Model-loss harm of SAE reconstructions compared with equal-norm random errors. This is only cited from Gurnee.
Split of the error into linear and nonlinear parts, and whether each responds to further dictionary learning. The curvature-residual account is theory, not a test.
Loss of circuit or steering behaviour when the error term is dropped.
No comparison of objectives, architectures or training budgets. The authors leave TopK and end-to-end SAEs open and note that the released SAEs are trained on a width-dependent token budget.

missing.what: Fitted floors at other sparsities (k=32, 64, 75), all positive with the ordering preserved; e.g. 9B L20 B=0.111/0.092/0.089.
Observed NMSE by dictionary width up to 1024K at the showcase layers, still non-zero at the largest width.

record.verdict_notes: The record's main error is linking the geometry regressions to V2; they measure a different construct. The floor evidence has a caveat. Drops by the monotone filter concentrate at the 524K and 1M widths, which the authors attribute to these SAEs being under-trained relative to a convergence budget. That could raise the fitted floors, a point relevant to V6, but the study does not test it. The study cites the original (Engels et al.) and Gurnee only as background.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a large share of the SAE error vector is linearly predictable from the input activation.

The paper studies aggregate checkpoint-level reconstruction loss and width-scaling exponents, not token-by-token error-norm predictability across SAE sizes or whether larger and smaller SAEs fail on the same contexts. Floors are identifiable only at six showcase layers.
Whether SAE reconstructions harm model loss more than equal-sized random errors.
Whether the linear and nonlinear error components correspond to unlearned features and qualitatively distinct residual structure.
Whether SAE-feature analyses lose a measurable share of model behaviour without the error term.

The paper notes the released SAEs' width-dependent training budgets, but does not compare training objectives, architectures, or schedules to test whether training artifacts explain or remove the observed scaling and floors.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 9B
rows.operation_detail: Regressed per-layer width-scaling exponent α(k=50) on multi-scale curvature; reported leave-one-layer-out R².
rows.measure: LOO R² for predicting per-layer SAE width-scaling exponent from curvature
rows.note: This supports predictable variation in aggregate SAE width-scaling across layers, but does not establish token-level error predictability or shared failure contexts.
rows.check: Measures how well manifold curvature predicts the per-layer width exponent across layers. V2 is about per-token error norms being predictable across SAE sizes, so this is a different construct. Belongs in fits_no_version.

labels.reason: R3–R8 give positive fitted floors at all six specified layers, supporting V2's width-persistence component under these fitting and training conditions. Cross-size token-level predictability remains untested.

relation.reason: The study reports its own reconstruction-loss fits bearing directly on whether error persists as dictionary width increases at fixed sparsity.

tranche.reason: Joint width–sparsity surface fits test the nonvanishing-error component of V2 through aggregate reconstruction floors, using a different method from cross-size token-error prediction.

source_check.notes: Floors are fitted extrapolations from filtered checkpoint data under a width-dependent training schedule, not direct observations at infinite width. Zero is a conceptual reference, not a reported baseline measurement; the paper reports code availability.

statements.correction: Section 4 reports source code released in an anonymous repository for surface fitting, regressions, validation, floor calibration, figures and tables; repository availability was not independently checked.
statements.problem: The six floors and their conditions are correct, but the assertion that no code is provided contradicts Section 4.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Aggregate reconstruction-loss scaling and fitted floors at the tested Gemma 2 layers/settings
reader_labels.reason: The geometry-based fits predict layerwise width-scaling exponents, and fitted floors are positive at the six showcase layers; see R1–R14.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The floor is identifiable and reported only at six showcase layers; the other layers use no-floor fits because their width grids are insufficient for floor identification (R3–R8).
